The Myth of Overparameterization
deep Manifold
@BetaTomorrow
·
Sep 1
·
1.1K
Chinese Edition:
关于过度参数化的误区
Modern neural networks are commonly described as overparameterized because they contain far more trainable parameters than traditional statistical models, and often more parameters than training examples. Yet these models can fit their training data closely while still generalizing well. This apparent contradiction has motivated extensive research into benign overfitting, double descent, implicit bias, feature learning, and training dynamics. So far, however, there is still no convincing theory that explains overparameterization clearly and fundamentally.
The discussion, however, rests on an assumption that is rarely examined: calling a model overparameterized implies that we already know approximately how many degrees of freedom the learning problem requires. In most cases, we do not. A large parameter count tells us how much computational freedom has been made available to learning, but it does not tell us how much freedom the problem itself requires.

Learning Is an Inverse Problem

The reason is fundamental. Learning is an inverse problem. We begin with data and boundary conditions and attempt to recover relationships that are not known beforehand. The structure to be learned is therefore part of the unknown solution.
Its required degrees of freedom are unknown for the same reason. Before learning, we do not know the full complexity of the relationships, their interactions, their discontinuities, or the amount of freedom needed to represent them adequately.
Neural networks are therefore given large parameter budgets deliberately. Too little freedom may prevent the required structure from forming, while the minimum sufficient amount cannot generally be determined in advance. What is called overparameterization is, in this sense, largely a practical safety margin for solving an unknown inverse problem.

Larger Models, Higher Risk of Babuška’s Paradox

More degrees of freedom give a model more capacity to learn, but they also create more possible computational pathways. When the learning space and boundary conditions are not sufficiently constrained, a larger model has more ways to form a plausible but incorrect solution.
A recent paper,
Zero-Shot Coordination among LLM Agents
, provides an interesting example. The authors found that smaller models such as Qwen3-14B and OLMo-3-32B-Think could recover the robust zero-shot coordination strategy, while several larger frontier models failed. Qwen3-Max-Thinking, with roughly one trillion parameters, performed significantly worse than Qwen3-14B in this setting. More reasoning effort could also reduce coordination performance by encouraging models to hallucinate a shared convention that did not actually exist.
Click the image to view the detail
This resembles the phenomenon discussed in
Zienkiewicz Moment, History Repeating Itself?
. Babuška’s paradox showed that increasing numerical refinement does not necessarily move a solution closer to the correct physical answer when the underlying formulation or boundary treatment is inadequate. More degrees of freedom can produce a more detailed approximation of the wrong solution.
The analogy should not be taken to mean that larger models are inherently worse. Rather, as available degrees of freedom increase, correct mathematical constraints become increasingly important. Scale expands what a model can learn, but it also expands the space of incorrect relationships and pathways that it can construct.
The larger the model, therefore, the greater the potential for a Babuška-like effect when the learning problem is inadequately constrained: more parameters and more reasoning may produce more computation without producing a more correct solution.

What to Learn Matters

The required degrees of freedom depend not only on the amount of data, but also on what we want to learn from the data. What we want to learn defines the learning space; the data alone does not. This distinction is discussed in
Mathematical Considerations for Learning Space
.
ImageNet provides a simple example. The same collection of images could be used to learn a coarse distinction such as indoor versus outdoor, or to distinguish among roughly twenty thousand categories. The underlying images may be largely the same, but the two tasks define very different learning spaces and therefore may require very different degrees of freedom.
The relevant capacity cannot be inferred from dataset size alone. What we ask the model to learn determines the learning space, and the learning space determines how much freedom may be required. Because learning is an inverse problem, that requirement is generally unknown before learning begins.

The Opportunity

The myth is not that neural networks are large. The myth is that we already know they contain too many parameters. Before learning, we do not know how many degrees of freedom the learning problem requires, so a large parameter budget is a reasonable design choice.
The opportunity appears after training. Once learning is complete, the unknown structure has already formed, and the question changes from how much freedom is needed to learn to how much of that freedom is still needed to preserve what has been learned.
Most previous efforts have approached this through pruning, quantization, low-rank approximation, or other forms of compression, with mixed results. These methods usually operate on weights, matrices, layers, or statistical importance, but they do not explicitly ask whether the learned manifold and its homological structure are being preserved.
From the Deep Manifold perspective, this may be the more important question. If training forms a connected piecewise manifold, parameter reduction should not simply remove weights that appear small or redundant. It should preserve the relationships, connectivity, and homology of the learned manifold.
The real opportunity, therefore, may not be to avoid overparameterization during learning, but to learn with sufficient freedom first, then reduce parameters while preserving the structure that learning has formed.
